qs.q: Which of the following shared genetic mutations is commonly found in both fibroadenomas of the breast and uterine leiomyomas?
o: Mutations within the TERT promoter region
Mutations involving the BRCA1 gene locus
Mutations affecting the MED12 gene sequence
Mutations occurring in the PIK3CA gene
qs.e: Both fibroadenomas and phyllodes tumors are driven by mutations in the MED12 gene, which is also mutated in uterine fibroids due to their shared hormone-sensitive stromal origin. TERT mutations are instead acquired in malignant phyllodes tumors.

qs.q: A pregnant woman develops sudden, severe abdominal pain due to a uterine leiomyoma undergoing hemorrhagic infarction. What type of degeneration has occurred?
qs.e: Red or carneous degeneration is a form of hemorrhagic infarction that classically occurs in uterine leiomyomas during pregnancy. Hyaline degeneration is much more common and presents with homogenous pink areas rather than infarction.

ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Uterine leiomyoma is a common benign smooth‑muscle tumour that grows with estrogen and can cause heavy bleeding, pain or infertility. Diagnosis relies on imaging and clinical history, and treatment ranges from watchful waiting to surgery.

sections.p: Leiomyomas are benign, well‑circumscribed smooth‑muscle nodules in the myometrium. They are diagnosed clinically by symptoms and confirmed with pelvic ultrasound or MRI, which shows whorled, hypoechoic masses.
The FIGO system stages fibroids by size and location: 0 (none) to 8 (large, multiple, intramural). Staging guides treatment urgency.

t.b: Detects size, number and location of fibroids; a large intramural or submucosal fibroid explains heavy bleeding.
Used when ultrasound is inconclusive or for pre‑operative planning; shows detailed anatomy and vascularity.

sections.p: The exact cause is unknown, but estrogen, progesterone, growth factors and genetic alterations (e.g., MED12 mutations) are implicated. Risk factors include early menarche, obesity and family history.

t.b: High levels during reproductive years promote growth; normal post‑menopause levels correlate with regression.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with menorrhagia, pelvic pressure, dysmenorrhoea, infertility or urinary symptoms if large.

t.b: Frequency and volume of bleeding help estimate fibroid size.

sections.p: Imaging is central; laboratory tests rule out mimics and assess complications.

t.b: Checks for anemia from chronic bleeding.
Low levels may indicate submucosal fibroids causing amenorrhoea.
Screening in low‑resource settings to avoid post‑operative complications.

sections.p: Acute pain, rapid enlargement, anemia, obstruction of the urinary tract, or sudden bleeding warrant urgent care.

t.b: Detects calcified fibroids in advanced degeneration.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first: hormonal therapy to shrink fibroids, then consider surgery or minimally invasive procedures. Choice depends on size, location, symptoms and fertility wishes.

t.b: Reduces estrogen, shrinking fibroids; used pre‑op to reduce size.
Blocks blood supply, causing fibroid shrinkage; suitable for women not seeking fertility.

sections.p: Regular pelvic exams and ultrasound every 1–2 years in symptomatic women. Lifestyle measures (weight control, balanced diet) may reduce risk.

t.b: Detects new or enlarging fibroids early.

sections.p: Endometrial carcinoma, adenomyosis, ovarian cysts, and uterine sarcoma can mimic fibroids clinically or on imaging.
Small submucosal fibroids may be missed on trans‑abdominal ultrasound; normal serum estradiol does not rule out fibroids.
